realism_constraints: No advanced forensic DNA or electronic surveillance technology
Limited rapid communication, reliance on telegrams and letters
Transportation mainly by train, horse-drawn vehicles, early motor cars
location: England, various locations including London, Rutlandshire, Cliffhurst, Netherhempsfield
institution: Private inquiry agents and police (Scotland Yard), Home Office
crime_subtype: the Virginiola book theft and recovery scheme

cast.name: Max Carrados
cast.role_archetype: blind amateur criminologist with exceptional senses
cast.public_persona: blind gentleman with wide interests and social connections
cast.private_secret: exceptional observational and deductive abilities despite blindness
cast.motive_seed: intellectual curiosity and sense of justice

cast.name: Louis Carlyle
cast.role_archetype: private inquiry agent, friend and assistant to Carrados
cast.private_secret: former solicitor with a past indiscretion

cast.name: Mr Marrable
cast.private_secret: keen on rare books and antiques

cast.name: Mr Powis
cast.private_secret: involved unknowingly in the book recovery

cast.name: Mr Chatton
cast.private_secret: orchestrated the theft and recovery of the Virginiola

surface_summary: A valuable rare book, the Virginiola, is stolen from a private library and sold at auction as an imperfect copy. The book mysteriously disappears after the sale, leading to suspicion and investigation involving dealers and the library secretary.
accepted_facts: The Virginiola book was sold at auction as an imperfect copy
The book was misdelivered to a purchaser who took it away
A second copy of the Virginiola was held by a bookseller Mr Powis
The secretary Mr Chatton had access to both copies and the library
inferred_conclusions: The purchaser who took the book away was the thief
Mr Powis knowingly dealt in stolen property
The book was lost due to clerical error at the auction house
mechanism_description: Mr Chatton, the secretary, secretly sold the original Virginiola before the library sale and then arranged to recover the stolen book by manipulating the auction and delivery notes. He temporarily removed identifying pages to disguise the book and returned it to the bookseller Mr Powis to avoid suspicion.
delivery_path: Mr Chatton sells the original Virginiola secretly before the auction
He sends a list of books including the Virginiola to the auction house
The auction house mistakenly delivers the stolen book to a purchaser
The purchaser unknowingly takes the stolen book away
Mr Chatton arranges for the stolen book to be returned to Mr Powis
The identifying pages are replaced and the book is disguised
Mr Powis holds the book as legitimate property, unaware of the theft
outcome_result: The stolen Virginiola is recovered and the secretary Mr Chatton is exposed as the culprit.

false_assumption.statement: The purchaser who took the book away at auction was the thief.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The purchaser physically took possession of the book and disappeared with it, making him the obvious suspect. The auction house's delivery note supported this assumption.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It hides the fact that the secretary orchestrated the theft and recovery, using the purchaser as an unwitting pawn.

supporting_points: Mr Powis had possession of a copy of the Virginiola
He was reluctant to show a receipt for the book
His name was connected with a stolen copy
He was suspected due to the timing of the book's return
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Mr Powis was unaware of the theft and acted in good faith

red_herrings.description: The large man who bought the lot at auction and took away the book
red_herrings.points_at_suspect: He physically took the book and disappeared
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He was an unwitting purchaser who received the stolen book due to a delivery note error

red_herrings.description: Suspicion around Mr Powis due to rumors and his reluctance to produce a receipt
red_herrings.points_at_suspect: His behavior suggested guilt and involvement
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He was a legitimate bookseller who was the victim of a malicious rumor and the secretary's scheme

closed_circle.rationale: Only these individuals had access to the book, the library, or the auction house during the relevant times, and the delivery notes and auction records limited the circle.

inference_path.observation: The delivery note was incorrectly filled out as Lot 191 instead of Lot 91
inference_path.correction: The purchaser took away the wrong lot
inference_path.effect: The stolen book was mistakenly delivered to the purchaser
required_evidence: Delivery note showing Lot 191 instead of Lot 91
Auction house clerk testimony about delivery note filling

inference_path.observation: Mr Powis had a copy of the Virginiola returned to him
inference_path.correction: The returned book was the stolen one
inference_path.effect: The stolen book was recovered and disguised
required_evidence: Mr Powis's statement about receiving the book back
Physical examination of the book showing replaced pages

inference_path.observation: Mr Chatton had sent lists to dealers and arranged approvals
inference_path.correction: He orchestrated the theft and recovery
inference_path.effect: Mr Chatton is the mastermind behind the scheme
required_evidence: Correspondence from Mr Chatton to dealers
Testimony about Mr Chatton's financial difficulties

inference_path.observation: The missing pages on the auction copy matched those in Mr Powis's copy
inference_path.correction: Pages were temporarily removed and replaced
inference_path.effect: The stolen book was disguised to avoid detection
required_evidence: Physical comparison of pages between copies
Expert testimony on book binding and restoration

inference_path.observation: Mr Chatton had access to the library and the books
inference_path.correction: He had opportunity to steal and manipulate the books
inference_path.effect: Opportunity for the crime is established
required_evidence: Witness statements about Mr Chatton's movements

inference_path.observation: No evidence of forced entry or other suspects
inference_path.correction: The crime was an inside job
inference_path.effect: Focus on library staff and dealers

inference_path.observation: Mr Powis was reluctant to produce a receipt
inference_path.correction: He feared suspicion but was innocent
inference_path.effect: Mr Powis is cleared as a suspect
required_evidence: Mr Powis's explanation of the missing receipt
Confirmation of legitimate purchase from Mr Winch

discriminating_test.design: Investigators verify the delivery notes and auction records to confirm the lot numbers and purchasers. They compare the physical copies of the Virginiola held by Mr Powis and the auction house to detect any alterations or missing pages. They also examine library access logs and correspondences to establish who had opportunity to manipulate the books.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: This test reveals that the stolen book was sold before the auction and then recovered and disguised by the secretary, Mr Chatton.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: Confirmation that the auction delivery note was falsified and that the book held by Mr Powis matches the stolen copy with replaced pages.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of the auction, the delivery notes, the booksellers involved, and the secretary's suspicious behavior. The physical evidence of missing and replaced pages is described, and the timing of events is clear. The false assumption about the purchaser is explicitly presented and can be questioned. The clues about Mr Chatton's financial motives and access are available for deduction.

anchors.claim: The auctioneer announced Lot 191 as imperfect and sold it
anchors.anchor: Lot 191 is imperfect and is sold not subject to return

anchors.claim: The delivery note was mistakenly filled as Lot 191 instead of Lot 91
anchors.anchor: sale clerk, in the stress of his duties, inadvertently filled in the delivery note as Lot 191

anchors.claim: Mr Powis received back the Virginiola book with formal regrets
anchors.anchor: the book was returned to me this morning

anchors.claim: Mr Chatton wrote to dealers pretending to buy a copy for collation
anchors.anchor: I wrote to a few dealers, rather, I am afraid, giving them the impression that we wished to buy a copy

anchors.claim: Mr Chatton secretly sold the original Virginiola before the auction
anchors.anchor: he had already sold the Virginiola himself only a week before

anchors.claim: The stolen book was disguised by removing and replacing pages
anchors.anchor: the abstracted sheet was cunningly replaced, probably certain erasable marks that had been put in for fuller disguise were removed

anchors.claim: Mr Powis did not have a receipt for the book because it was paid by cheque initialed to bearer
anchors.anchor: I was making out a cheque when he reminded me that his right hand was useless and asked me to initial it to ‘bearer.’ That is why I come to have no receipt

anchors.claim: The purchaser took away the wrong lot due to delivery note error
anchors.anchor: Another purchaser bought certain lots. Among them was Lot 91. My sale clerk... inadvertently filled in the delivery note as Lot 191

anchors.claim: Mr Chatton’s motive was financial need and deception
anchors.anchor: he had expenses. Perhaps he had fallen into the hands of the Jews; perhaps it was the Jewesses

anchors.claim: The auction house was slow to turn the case over to the police
anchors.anchor: you will find more profit in investigating farther afield

anchors.claim: Mr Marrable was interested in the Virginiola and its market value
anchors.anchor: I should certainly like to land the Virginiola

anchors.claim: The stolen book was sold as imperfect to reduce suspicion
anchors.anchor: if at the sale it was discovered to be imperfect in an important detail then it might realise only a fraction of that sum

anchors.claim: Mr Powis was worried about rumors affecting his business
anchors.anchor: My name has been connected with a stolen copy and buyers are very shy

anchors.claim: Mr Chatton’s scheme involved buying back the book before the sale
anchors.anchor: The first thing was to get back the Virginiola a little before the sale

anchors.claim: Mr Chatton’s plan failed because the market value had risen
anchors.anchor: What he had not taken into account was the enormous rise in the value of this class of work

anchors.claim: The secretary’s scheme was speculative and left no evidence
anchors.anchor: Chatton... did not leave behind him one solitary shred of evidence that would stand before a jury

anchors.claim: Mr Carrados advised the auction house to verify the stolen book’s status
anchors.anchor: I would suggest that we eliminate Mr Dillworthy... What remains?

anchors.claim: The purchaser’s buying pattern was suspicious but not conclusive
anchors.anchor: Mr Dillworthy bought 91 at a good price. After that he did nothing until 191 had passed. Then he secured four lots of cheap books

anchors.claim: The purchaser declined to write his name on the back of a banknote
anchors.anchor: He held out a bank-note... I gave him a pen... He handed me the pen back and said: ‘Thanks; after all, I’ll leave it as it is.’
